title: Redis Cluster and production operations
goal: By the end you can predict which node of a Redis Cluster holds a key, keep the keys that change together in one slot, explain what a client does on MOVED and ASK, and find the command, fork or key behind a latency spike on any Redis.

warmup.q: A Redis Cluster has three primaries. Over a plain connection to node 1 you send `MSET payment:42 approved payment:43 approved`. payment:42 hashes to a slot on node 2 and payment:43 to a slot on node 3. What comes back?
options: OK: node 1 forwards each key to its owner
MOVED, pointing at node 2, the owner of the first key
CROSSSLOT: the keys are in different slots, so no node can run the command
OK, but only payment:42 is written
warmup.why: Cluster nodes never forward commands. A node first checks that all the keys of a command are in one slot. These two aren't (slots 9055 and 13182), so it refuses with `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot` before it even looks at who owns them. A single-key command for node 2's slot would have got MOVED. Some cluster clients split such an MSET into one command per slot themselves, which works, but the two halves are no longer one atomic step.

sections.h: One server has one thread and one machine's memory, so split the keys
sections.body:
Lesson 9 made copies of one Redis, and copies don't make it bigger. The idempotency store from lesson 5 keeps growing. Add rate limits, sessions and a cache of fraud features, and one Redis needs 40 GB of memory and 300,000 commands a second. Another replica doesn't help: it copies every key and every write, so it splits neither the memory nor the work. And lesson 2's model sets the ceiling, one thread running every command of one server. You need several primaries, each owning part of the keys. How to split data across machines in general (key ranges against hashes, rebalancing, routing, hot keys) is the Partitioning track's subject in the next part. This lesson is Redis's own answer, and the operations work that comes with running it.

The simplest split lives in the client: choose a server with `hash(key) mod N`. It works until N changes. Go from 3 servers to 4, and a key stays where it was only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 3 and for 4. Over 1,000,000 keys from `payment:1` to `payment:1000000`, 75% landed on a different server. Each of those is a cache miss, or worse, an idempotency key that seems to have vanished.

Redis Cluster puts a fixed layer in between. The keyspace has 16,384 **hash slots**, and a key's slot is `CRC16(key) mod 16384`. CRC16 is a 16-bit checksum, a number computed from the key's bytes; it is cheap, and its results spread evenly, so keys spread evenly over the slots. The number of slots never changes. What changes is the slot table, which says which primary owns each slot. Three primaries split it into 0-5460, 5461-10922 and 10923-16383. Adding a fourth moves 4,096 slots to it, about 1,365 from each of the others, and only the keys in those slots move: 25%, the least possible for a node that should hold a quarter of the data.

That gives this lesson's model: **a key hashes to a slot, and a slot belongs to one primary.** Every rule that follows comes from that chain: where a command must go, which keys one command can use together, and what moves when the cluster grows or a node fails. Every node knows the whole slot table. The nodes keep it in step by talking to each other on a second port, the cluster bus, which is the client port plus 10,000.

try.title: Ask a real cluster where keys live
steps: From the `labs` folder, start a three-node cluster: `docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml up -d --wait`. The nodes listen on 7001, 7002 and 7003, and a one-off container joined them and split the slots. Open a prompt on node 1: `docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml exec node-1 redis-cli -p 7001`.
Before each `CLUSTER KEYSLOT`, say which node you expect to own the slot, using the three ranges above.
Read `CLUSTER SHARDS`: one entry per primary, with its slot range and its address. Leave the cluster running for the rest of the lesson.

code.title: at node 1's redis-cli prompt
code.src:
CLUSTER INFO
CLUSTER KEYSLOT payment:42
CLUSTER KEYSLOT payment:43
CLUSTER KEYSLOT 123456789
CLUSTER SHARDS

try.expect: `CLUSTER INFO` starts with `cluster_state:ok` and `cluster_slots_assigned:16384`, and further down shows `cluster_known_nodes:3` and `cluster_size:3`. `payment:42` is in slot `9055` (node 2's range) and `payment:43` in `13182` (node 3's). `123456789` is in `12739`: the cluster spec's test string, whose CRC16 is 0x31C3, 12,739, already below 16,384. `CLUSTER SHARDS` lists each primary's `slots` pair, such as `10923` and `16383`, then its `id`, `port 7003`, `ip 127.0.0.1` and `role master`. The node ids are random 40-character strings and differ on every run.

refs.title: Redis cluster specification: key distribution model

sections.h: A node that doesn't own the slot sends you to the one that does
sections.body:
Send `GET payment:42` to node 1 with a plain client, and the answer is an error: `MOVED 9055 127.0.0.1:7002`. Slot 9055 lives on 127.0.0.1:7002; ask there. The node doesn't forward the command for you. Cluster nodes never proxy, so each node only ever works on its own slots.

The simplest client follows every MOVED, which costs a second round trip for about two keys in three. A **cluster-aware client** does better. When it starts, it asks any node for the whole slot table (`CLUSTER SHARDS`, or the older `CLUSTER SLOTS`), keeps connections to every node, computes each key's slot itself and sends each command straight to the owner. A MOVED then becomes rare, and it means the table changed: a slot moved, or a replica took over from a dead primary. The client updates its table, usually by reloading all of it, because a slot rarely moves alone. Jedis's `RedisClusterClient` and Lettuce's `RedisClusterClient` both work this way, and Lettuce 7 also refreshes its table when it notices redirects.

Because the client does the routing, the address in a MOVED reply must work from wherever the client runs. Each node announces one address, and that is behind most "the cluster works inside Docker but not from my laptop" problems: the nodes announce container addresses that the Mac can't reach. The lab's Compose file runs all three nodes in one network namespace and announces 127.0.0.1 (`cluster-announce-ip`), so the same address works inside Docker and from the Mac. In Kubernetes the same choice shows up as pod IPs or hostnames.

Pipelines follow the same rule: a cluster client splits one pipeline into one per node. A MULTI/EXEC transaction can't be split across nodes, which brings up the next section's rule.

stepper.title: From key to slot to node, and what MOVED fixes
stepper.intro: Three primaries with the slot ranges `redis-cli --cluster create` gave them, and two kinds of client.

frames.say: Every key maps to one slot, and anyone can compute it. CRC16 of `payment:42` is 58,207; modulo 16,384 that is slot 9055. No server is involved, which is why a client can route commands itself.

frames.say: Node 1 owns slots 0 to 5460, not 9055. It doesn't forward the command. It answers with an error that names the slot and its owner: `MOVED 9055 127.0.0.1:7002`. The client must ask again, at that address.

sections.h: Keys that must change together need the same slot
sections.body:
Send `MSET payment:42 approved payment:43 approved` to a node and it refuses: `CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot`. The two keys live in slots 9055 and 13182, on different nodes, and no node can change keys it doesn't hold in one atomic step. The rule covers every command that names several keys (MSET, MGET, SUNIONSTORE, RENAME), every MULTI/EXEC transaction and every Lua script. A Lua script that moves money from `acct:a` to `acct:b` fails on a cluster as written, and so does lesson 7's lease fill if its two keys lose their shared tag. Even two slots that happen to sit on the same node are refused, because either one could move tomorrow.

Cluster clients can hide this. In the demo, Jedis and Lettuce both accepted the cross-slot MSET by splitting it into one MSET per slot and sending each half to its node. Each half is atomic; the pair isn't, and a crash between them leaves one payment approved and the other not.

The fix is a **hash tag**. If a key contains `{`, then a `}` after it, with at least one character between them, only the part between the first `{` and the next `}` is hashed. `{merchant:7}:payments` and `{merchant:7}:refunds` both hash `merchant:7`, both land in slot 10890, and MSET, MULTI and scripts work on them again. Tag by the smallest unit that must change atomically: the customer whose two accounts a transfer touches, or a payment and its refunds. Tagging by tenant is the classic mistake. A merchant with 40% of the traffic then puts 40% of the load on one slot, so on one node, and adding nodes won't help.

Slots move: to add a node, to drain one, to even out load. The classic way marks the slot MIGRATING on the source and IMPORTING on the target, then copies its keys in batches with MIGRATE. Meanwhile the source still serves the keys it has, and for a key it doesn't have it answers `ASK 9055 127.0.0.1:7003`: send this one command there, after an ASKING command, but leave your table alone, since the slot hasn't moved yet. A multi-key command whose keys are split between the two nodes gets `TRYAGAIN`. Redis 8.4 added atomic slot migration: `CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT` on the target copies the whole slot, a snapshot plus the writes that arrive meanwhile, then switches the owner in one step. In the lab it moved 1,001 keys in 31 ms with no write pause.

A cluster also does Sentinel's job. Give each primary a replica; when a primary is unreachable for `cluster-node-timeout`, the other primaries vote and its replica takes over its slots. Sentinel protects one primary that holds everything. Cluster splits the data and fails over each part on its own.

try.title: Refuse, tag, and move a slot
steps: At the cluster-aware prompt (`docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml exec node-1 redis-cli -c -p 7001`), try the cross-slot MSET, find the hash tag's slot, and write two tagged keys in one MSET.

From a second terminal in the `labs` folder, run the script in part 2. It marks slot 9055 as moving from node 2 to node 3, asks both nodes for a key that isn't on node 2, then cancels the move with `STABLE`. Predict the three GET answers first. The script's output has no `(error)` prefix, because redis-cli prints plain text when it isn't talking to a terminal.

Move slot 10890 for real with atomic slot migration (part 3), read the task's status, and ask node 1 for a tagged key. Stop the cluster when you are done: `docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml down -v`.

code.src:
MSET payment:42 a payment:43 b
CLUSTER KEYSLOT {merchant:7}:payments
MSET {merchant:7}:payments 10 {merchant:7}:refunds 2

# 2. an ASK during a classic migration, then cancel it
docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml exec node-1 sh -c '
  N2=$(redis-cli -p 7002 CLUSTER MYID); N3=$(redis-cli -p 7003 CLUSTER MYID)
  redis-cli -p 7003 CLUSTER SETSLOT 9055 IMPORTING $N2
  redis-cli -p 7002 CLUSTER SETSLOT 9055 MIGRATING $N3
  redis-cli -p 7002 GET payment:42
  redis-cli -p 7002 GET {payment:42}:refund
  redis-cli -p 7003 GET {payment:42}:refund
  redis-cli -p 7002 CLUSTER SETSLOT 9055 STABLE
  redis-cli -p 7003 CLUSTER SETSLOT 9055 STABLE'

# 3. atomic slot migration (Redis 8.4): node 3 imports slot 10890

docker compose -f env/redis-cluster.yml exec node-1 redis-cli -p 7003 CLUSTER MIGRATION STATUS ALL

try.expect: The cross-slot MSET fails with `(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot`: the node checks the slots before it looks at who owns them. `CLUSTER KEYSLOT {merchant:7}:payments` prints `(integer) 10890`, and the tagged MSET prints `-> Redirected to slot [10890] located at 127.0.0.1:7002` and `OK`. The script prints `OK` twice, then `settled` (node 2 still has payment:42, last written by the demo's MSET, so it serves it; `approved` if you skipped the demo), `ASK 9055 127.0.0.1:7003` (node 2 doesn't have the refund key, so it points at the importing node), and from node 3 `MOVED 9055 127.0.0.1:7002`, because that request came without ASKING. `CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT` returns a task id such as `"990e869ed5f96033ff939b837141264751b539fa"`. The status shows `slots` `10890-10890`, `operation` `import`, `state` `completed`, `retries` `0` and `write_pause_ms` `0`; my run took 61 ms from `start_time` to `end_time`. Node 1 now answers `(error) MOVED 10890 127.0.0.1:7003`.

sections.h: When every client slows down at once, find the one slow command
sections.body:
The pattern looks like this: the p99 of every service that uses a Redis jumps from 1 ms to 300 ms at the same moment, while the Redis host's CPU graph stays calm. Lesson 2 explains it. One thread runs every command, so one slow command delays everything queued behind it, whatever key it touches, and one busy core on a 16-core host barely moves the graph.

`KEYS` is the classic culprit. In the lab, `KEYS demo:l10:refund:*` matched nothing and still walked all 1,000,000 keys in one command: 150 to 340 ms, and a GET sent meanwhile from another thread waited just as long. `SCAN` does the same walk in slices. Each call visits roughly COUNT entries of the key table and returns a cursor for the next call, so other clients are served in between. A full SCAN with `COUNT 1000` took 1,000 calls and about 2 seconds in all, yet the slowest GET during it waited 16 to 27 ms on the same VM. The price is weaker promises: SCAN can return a key twice, and a key added during the walk may or may not appear. The same reasoning covers every command whose cost grows with the size of a key: `HGETALL`, `SMEMBERS` or `LRANGE 0 -1` on a big key (page with `HSCAN`, `SSCAN` or ranges), DEL of a big key (`UNLINK` frees it on a background thread), and long Lua scripts.

Redis keeps the evidence. The **slow log** holds the last 128 commands that ran longer than `slowlog-log-slower-than`, 10,000 microseconds by default. It times only the execution on the command thread, never network or queueing time; in the lab, `SLOWLOG GET` showed `KEYS demo:l10:refund:*` at 145,531 microseconds. The latency monitor (off by default; `CONFIG SET latency-monitor-threshold 10` turns it on) records events that aren't commands, such as a fork for BGSAVE (lesson 9), an AOF fsync that blocked, or a long expiry cycle (lesson 5), and `LATENCY DOCTOR` turns them into advice. `INFO commandstats` gives calls and microseconds per call for each command, which catches the case where no single command is slow but one runs a million times a minute.

When none of those show anything, measure the machine. `redis-cli --intrinsic-latency 100` measures how long the operating system keeps the Redis process from running at all. On the lab's Docker VM, shared with other courses' databases, the worst stall was about 50 ms: no command was slow, and still some replies waited that long.

sections.h: Big keys, hot keys, and memory that doesn't come back
sections.body:
Two kinds of key cause most of the remaining trouble, and both defeat the cluster's plan of spreading work over slots.

A **big key** is one key that grew: a merchant's hash with 200,000 payments, 9.6 MB in one key. Every O(N) command on it is slow, it sits on one node however large the cluster is, and moving its slot means copying it in one piece. `redis-cli --bigkeys` walks the keyspace with SCAN and reports the biggest key of each type by element count; `--memkeys` reports bytes. The fix is lesson 3's: split it, by day or by a hash of the payment id.

A **hot key** takes a large share of the traffic, such as the profile of your largest merchant, read on every authorization. It lives in one slot, so one node's thread serves all of it, and adding nodes changes nothing. Redis 8.6 added `HOTKEYS` to find them: `HOTKEYS START METRICS 2 CPU NET` records which keys use the most command-thread time and network bytes, and `HOTKEYS GET` reports them. In the lab one merchant profile took 35,266 of 42,732 microseconds of command time (83%) and 4.25 of 5.15 MB of traffic. The fixes: cache it in each pod (lesson 6's client-side caching), read it from replicas, or split a hot counter into several keys and add them up.

Memory has its own trap. `used_memory` is what Redis's allocator has handed out; `used_memory_rss` is what the kernel has given the process. Delete half your keys and the first drops while the second barely moves: the allocator keeps the freed pieces inside pages that still hold live values, and can't return a page until all of it is free (the Operating systems track's lesson on memory allocation, Memory allocation: malloc, arenas and why RSS grows). In the lab, 500,000 values of 100 bytes used 85 MB with an RSS of 101 MB. After deleting every other key: 50 MB used, RSS still 101 MB, a `mem_fragmentation_ratio` of 2.04. `CONFIG SET activedefrag yes` makes Redis move live values into fuller pages, a little at a time on the main thread; about 20 seconds later RSS was 70 MB and the ratio 1.42. On a nearly empty server the ratio means nothing, because a few fixed megabytes dominate it.

The last choice is which Redis to run. Redis was BSD-licensed up to 7.2; 7.4 moved to RSALv2 or SSPLv1, and 8.0 added AGPLv3 as a third option. In March 2024 the Linux Foundation forked Redis 7.2.4 as Valkey, BSD-licensed and backed by AWS, Google and Oracle among others; it is now at 9.1. Everything in this track up to Redis 7.2 works on both. Newer commands differ: DELEX, INCREX, HOTKEYS, CLUSTER MIGRATION and BACKUP are Redis 8, while Valkey 9.0 has its own atomic slot migration and allows numbered databases in cluster mode. Choose by the license your company accepts, the managed service your cloud runs, and which of those commands you need.

try.title: Find a big key and a hot key

From a second terminal in the `labs` folder, make one key hot and spread some other reads: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-benchmark -q -n 50000 GET merchant:7:profile`, then the same with `-n 20000 -r 300 GET payment:__rand_int__`. try.expect: The EVAL prints `(integer) 200000` and `MEMORY USAGE` about `(integer) 9634717`: 9.6 MB in one key. The benchmarks print lines like `GET merchant:7:profile: 24875.62 requests per second, p50=0.911 msec`. `HOTKEYS GET` (trimmed) shows `all-commands-all-slots-us` `42732` and `total-net-bytes` `5150000`, then under `by-cpu-time-us` first `"merchant:7:profile"` `35266`, far ahead of keys like `"payment:000000000022"` `489` (redis-benchmark pads the random numbers), and under `by-net-bytes` `"merchant:7:profile"` `4250000`. Your numbers differ; the order doesn't. `--bigkeys` ends with `Biggest   hash found "merchant:7:payments" has 200000 fields` and `Biggest string found "merchant:7:profile" has 40 bytes`; `--memkeys` reports the same hash as `9634717 bytes`. Both walk the keyspace with SCAN, so they are safe on a busy server.

analogy: A Redis Cluster is a warehouse with 16,384 numbered shelves spread over three buildings. Every parcel's label goes through the same formula to give a shelf number, so anyone can work out where a parcel belongs without asking. Each building keeps a map of which building holds which shelves. Walk into the wrong building and the clerk doesn't fetch your parcel: he points across the street (MOVED). While a shelf is being carried to another building, he points you there only for the parcels he no longer has (ASK), and your map stays as it was. Parcels that must be packed together carry the same name in braces, so they land on one shelf. The analogy breaks at the shelf move: real buildings move a shelf box by box, while Redis 8.4's atomic slot migration copies the shelf in the background and switches its owner in one step, so no client is ever told a parcel is in two places.
in_your_world: Before a payment service moves to Redis Cluster, or to a managed service that runs one, list its multi-key operations, because each of them now needs its keys in one slot: a Lua script that moves money between two keys, lesson 7's value and lease keys, lesson 8's idempotency record and its rate-limit counters, and any MULTI over several keys. Give each group a hash tag at the level that must change atomically, `{payment:p-981}` or `{customer:991}`, never the merchant or the tenant. Single-key commands keep working through a cluster-aware client with no code changes; the surprises are in scripts and transactions, so run the integration tests against three nodes (this lesson's Compose file is enough). For operations, put three numbers on the Redis dashboard next to your Kafka consumer lag: the slow log length (`SLOWLOG LEN`), `latest_fork_usec`, and `mem_fragmentation_ratio`. And reject `KEYS` in code review: the fraud team's nightly `KEYS fraud:*` is the same 300 ms pause for your authorization path that the demo measured, every night.
mistake: The most common mistake is moving to Redis Cluster for capacity and finding out in production that multi-key code breaks. A Lua script or a MULTI over keys in different slots fails with CROSSSLOT, or, quieter and worse, the client splits an MSET across nodes and a crash leaves half of it applied. It happens because a single Redis never enforced the rule, and the test environment runs a single Redis. Run the test suite against a three-node cluster, search the code for MULTI, EVAL, FCALL and multi-key commands, and give every group of keys that changes together a hash tag at the narrowest level that works. Then watch HOTKEYS or `CLUSTER SLOT-STATS` (Redis 8.4) for one slot taking most of the traffic, the sign that a tag was too wide.

compare.note: Both clients start from one seed node, load the slot table and route every command by slot. `{payment:p-981}` hashes to slot 445, so all of that payment's keys live on one node, and a script over them runs there as one step: both versions printed `1` (one key deleted) against the lab cluster. Neither client gives you MULTI on a cluster connection. Jedis 8's `RedisClusterClient.multi()` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, and Lettuce's cluster API has no `multi` at all; with Lettuce you can take one node's connection from `client.partitions` and run MULTI there, but a script over tagged keys is the portable way. Jedis blocks the calling thread for each call, while the Kotlin version suspends the coroutine and shares one connection per node among all callers.

(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

(integer) 5094

fun account(customerId: Long, name: String) = "{customer:$customerId}:$name"   // one tag per customer: one slot

val moved = cluster.eval(TRANSFER_SCRIPT,
    listOf(account(991, "main"), account(991, "savings")), listOf("3000"))

steps.say: A transfer between two customers has no common tag that wouldn't put everyone in one slot. So make it two single-slot steps that are each idempotent, keyed by the transfer id as in lesson 8: debit customer 991 with `t-77` recorded in its slot, then credit customer 412 with `t-77` recorded in its slot, retrying each until it reports done. If the money must never be visible in neither account, keep that transfer in the database (Oracle, for this team) and use Redis only for the fast checks around it.
steps.code:
debit  {customer:991}:main  by 3000 unless {customer:991}:done:t-77 exists   (one script, one slot)
credit {customer:412}:main  by 3000 unless {customer:412}:done:t-77 exists   (one script, another slot)

lab.title: Route keys like a cluster client, then find the slow command and the big key
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 17 fail: 11 in `ClusterRouterTest`, which needs no Docker because `ModelCluster.kt` (done for you) is a three-node cluster in memory, and 6 in `DiagnosticsTest`, which use the shared Redis container.

In `ClusterRouter.kt`, write `HashSlots.crc16`, `hashTag` and `slot`. Run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l10.ClusterRouterTest'`: the four slot tests pass. The numbers in `slots match what a real Redis 8 cluster answered` come from this lesson's Try its.
Read `ModelCluster.send`: it is how a real node chooses between running a command, MOVED, ASK, CROSSSLOT and TRYAGAIN. Then write `ClusterRouter.execute` and run the class again until all 11 pass.
In `Diagnostics.java`, write `slowest` (sort the slow log by time spent) and `biggestKeys` (SCAN with MATCH, then MEMORY USAGE per key). Run all 17 tests.
hints: CRC16, byte by byte: `crc = crc xor ((b.toInt() and 0xFF) shl 8)`, then 8 times `crc = if (crc and 0x8000 != 0) (crc shl 1) xor 0x1021 else crc shl 1`, then `crc = crc and 0xFFFF`.
`hashTag`: `val open = key.indexOf('{')`, then `key.indexOf('}', open + 1)`. Use the whole key if either is -1 or if the close comes right after the open.
In `execute`, keep `node` and `asking` in two `var`s and loop with `repeat(maxRedirects + 1)`. A `return` inside works, because `repeat` is inline.
In `biggestKeys`, keep a `Set` of keys you have seen, sort with `Comparator.comparingLong(BigKey::bytes).reversed()`, and return at most `n`.

drill.title: Slot math from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `hashTag(key)` and `slot(key)` from memory; you may call a `crc16(bytes)` you don't write. Then, without running anything, say which of these share a slot: `{merchant:7}:payments`, `merchant:7`, `{merchant:7`, `x{merchant:7}y`.

recap: Redis Cluster splits the keyspace into 16,384 slots: slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each slot belongs to one primary. Adding a fourth node moves only the slots it takes, 25% of the keys, against 75% with hash mod N.
A node that doesn't own a key's slot answers `MOVED <slot> <address>` and never forwards. Cluster-aware clients cache the slot table, route each command themselves and refresh the table on MOVED.

Multi-key commands, transactions and scripts need all their keys in one slot, or the node answers CROSSSLOT. A hash tag `{...}` hashes only the tagged part; tag by the smallest unit that must change atomically.
During a classic slot move, `ASK` sends one command to the target after ASKING and leaves the table alone. Redis 8.4's `CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT` moves a whole slot atomically.
When every client slows down at once, look for one slow command: SLOWLOG, the latency monitor, `INFO commandstats`, then `--intrinsic-latency`. SCAN instead of KEYS; UNLINK for big keys.
Find big keys with `--bigkeys` and `--memkeys` and hot keys with HOTKEYS (8.6). When RSS stays far above used memory after deletes, active defrag can give it back.

quiz.q: A cluster of 3 primaries holds 30 million keys. You add a fourth primary and rebalance so that each holds a quarter of the slots. About how many keys move?
options: None: every key keeps its slot
About 7.5 million: only the keys in the 4,096 slots handed to the new node
About 22.5 million, as with hash mod N
All 30 million, because the slot table changes
quiz.why: A key's slot never changes; what changes is the owner of 4,096 slots, about 1,365 taken from each old node. The keys in those slots, a quarter of all keys, move with them. With hash mod N, going from 3 servers to 4 moves three keys in four. The first option is half right: the slots stay, but some change owner, and their keys go along.

quiz.q: From lesson 7: the lease fill script reads the lease key and writes the value key in one EVAL. A teammate names them `merchant:m-17` and `lease:m-17`. What happens to the fill on a three-node cluster?
options: It fails with CROSSSLOT: without a shared hash tag the two names hash to different slots, and a script needs all its keys in one slot
It works: a script may touch keys on any node
It works, but the node first forwards the lease check to the node that owns the lease key
It fails only when the two slots happen to live on different nodes
quiz.why: Without braces the whole name is hashed, so the two keys almost always land in different slots, and a node refuses any script whose keys span slots, because it can't run it atomically. Even two slots on the same node are refused, since either could move tomorrow. Nodes never forward. Naming them `merchant:{m-17}` and `lease:{m-17}`, as the lab does, puts both in the slot of `m-17`.

quiz.q: During a classic resharding of slot 9055 from node 2 to node 3, your client sends `GET {payment:42}:refund` to node 2 and gets `ASK 9055 127.0.0.1:7003`. What should it do?
options: Map slot 9055 to node 3 and send every later slot-9055 command there
Retry on node 2 until the key shows up
Send ASKING and then the GET to node 3, this once, and keep sending other slot-9055 commands to node 2
Send the GET to node 3 without ASKING
quiz.why: ASK means the slot is on its way: this key is no longer, or not yet, on node 2, but other keys of the slot still are. So only this command goes to node 3, preceded by ASKING, which tells node 3 to serve a slot it is importing but doesn't own yet. Without ASKING, node 3 answers MOVED back to node 2. Updating the table is what MOVED asks for, once the move is finished.

quiz.q: Every service's p99 on one Redis jumps from 1 ms to 140 ms for a moment, about every 5 minutes. The slow log shows nothing. What do you check next?
options: Lower `slowlog-log-slower-than` to 1 ms so that smaller commands are logged too
Turn on io-threads
Replace KEYS with SCAN everywhere
The latency monitor and `latest_fork_usec`: a BGSAVE fork from the save points pauses the main thread, and the slow log only times commands
quiz.why: The slow log times command execution. The fork behind a BGSAVE (lesson 9) pauses the main thread outside any command, and the default save points fire every few minutes on a busy server. `INFO stats` shows `latest_fork_usec`, and with `latency-monitor-threshold` set, `LATENCY LATEST` records `fork` events. A lower threshold logs more commands, but still only commands, and I/O threads neither run commands nor fork.

quiz.q: A clean-up job must delete 2 million `tmp:*` keys from a production Redis that holds 30 million keys. Which approach keeps other clients fast?
options: SCAN with `MATCH tmp:* COUNT 1000`, and UNLINK each page of keys it returns
`KEYS tmp:*`, then DEL them in batches of 1,000
One Lua script that calls KEYS and DEL
FLUSHDB ASYNC
quiz.why: KEYS walks all 30 million keys in one command and blocks every client for seconds, whether a client or a script calls it. SCAN does the same walk in small steps with other commands served in between, and UNLINK frees each value on a background thread. FLUSHDB would delete the other 28 million keys too.

flashcards.front: How does Redis Cluster pick a key's slot?
flashcards.back: CRC16 (XMODEM) of the key, or of its hash tag, modulo 16,384.
MOVED: the slot lives elsewhere now, so update your table. ASK: the slot is moving, so send this one command to the target after ASKING, and keep your table.

flashcards.front: When is only part of a key hashed?
flashcards.back: When it has a `{`, a later `}`, and at least one character between: only the part between the first `{` and the next `}` is hashed.
A command, transaction or script named keys in more than one slot. No node can run it as one step.

flashcards.front: What does the slow log measure?
flashcards.back: Time a command spent executing on the main thread, for commands over `slowlog-log-slower-than` (10 ms by default). Not network time, not queueing, not forks.
KEYS walks the whole keyspace in one command and blocks every client. SCAN walks it in small steps with other commands in between, at the price of possible duplicates.

flashcards.front: What does a high `mem_fragmentation_ratio` mean after big deletes?
flashcards.back: RSS stayed while used memory fell: freed pieces are stuck in pages that still hold live values. Active defrag compacts them.

terms.plain: One of 16,384 buckets; a key's slot is CRC16 of the key (or its hash tag) mod 16384.
The map of which primary owns each slot; every node and every cluster-aware client keeps a copy.
A node's reply naming the slot's owner: the slot lives elsewhere, so ask there and update your table.
A node's reply during a slot move: send just this command to the target, after ASKING.
The part of a key between `{` and `}`; when present, only it is hashed, so related keys share a slot.
The last 128 commands that ran longer than a threshold on the command thread, with their arguments.
A single key holding so many elements or bytes that commands on it, or moving it, block the server.
A single key receiving a large share of the traffic, so one node's thread does most of the work.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate how a cluster-aware client finds the node for `GET {payment:p-981}:status`, what happens when a slot has moved since the client started, and why the braces are in the key name.
explain_back.answer: The client hashes the key. Because the name has braces with something inside, only `payment:p-981` is hashed: CRC16 of it, modulo 16,384, is slot 445. When the client started, it loaded the slot table from a node, so it looks up slot 445, finds the primary that owns it, and sends the GET straight there over its connection to that node. Nothing is forwarded between nodes. If an operator moved slot 445 since then, the old owner answers `MOVED 445` with the new address. The client retries there and fixes its table, usually by reloading the whole table, so later commands go straight to the new owner. If the slot is in the middle of a move, the old owner may answer ASK instead, for keys it no longer has: the client sends just that one command to the new node, after ASKING, and leaves its table alone. The braces exist so that every key of this payment, its status, its attempts counter and its refunds, lands in the same slot. Then one MULTI or one Lua script can change them together, which a cluster refuses with CROSSSLOT when keys are in different slots. We tag by payment, not by merchant, so that one big merchant doesn't pile all its traffic onto one slot and one node.

deeper.body:
**Reading from replicas.** A cluster replica redirects every command to its primary unless the connection sends `READONLY` first; then it serves reads for its primary's slots, a little behind as lesson 9 explained. Both Jedis and Lettuce can route reads to replicas (Lettuce's `ReadFrom` setting), which spreads a hot key's reads over more threads.

**Per-slot numbers.** Redis 8.4 added `CLUSTER SLOT-STATS`, which reports per slot how many keys it holds and how much CPU time and network traffic it used. It answers the question HOTKEYS answers for keys, one level up: which slot, and so which hash tag, is too hot.

**Pub/sub on a cluster.** A plain `PUBLISH` is copied to every node in the cluster, because a subscriber can be connected anywhere. Sharded pub/sub (`SPUBLISH`, `SSUBSCRIBE`, Redis 7.0) assigns each channel to a slot like a key, so a message travels only within that slot's shard. Notifications that fan out to many pods belong there on a cluster.

**One database only.** Redis Cluster supports only database 0, so `SELECT 1` fails; separate data with key prefixes or separate clusters. Valkey 9.0 lifted that limit for its own cluster mode.

**Write safety in a split.** The cluster spec is open about losses: replication is asynchronous, so a primary can acknowledge a write and fail before its replica has it, and a primary cut off on the minority side of a network split keeps taking writes until `cluster-node-timeout` passes, then refuses them. Writes made there in that window are lost when the majority side promotes its replica. That is lesson 9's failover story again, per shard.

**Valkey in practice.** Valkey publishes the image `valkey/valkey`, and its CLI is `valkey-cli`, which accepts the same commands. The two have changed separately since 2024, so treat a move between them as a migration: test it with your own data and commands rather than assume a file copied from one loads in the other.

**The general picture.** Redis Cluster is one point in a larger design space: a fixed number of hash slots, assigned by hand or by a tool, with clients that route by a cached table. The Partitioning track compares it with key-range splits, consistent hashing, automatic rebalancing and routing tiers, and its lessons on Cassandra, MongoDB and DynamoDB show the same questions answered differently.
